fields.meta_title: Overtime Request Form With Hour Caps and Costs | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an overtime request form that shows each request's cost and weekly total, then holds anything past your cap before a manager approves.
fields.h1: Build an Overtime Request Form That Checks Hours and Cost
fields.hero_description: An overtime request form asks for approval before someone works extra hours. Emergent builds one that prices those hours and sends each request to whoever owns the budget.
fields.features_heading: What the Approver Sees Before Saying Yes
fields.features_subheading: Paper forms stop at a signature line. Emergent's version shows what the hours do to the week and the budget first.
fields.feature_1:
The week's hours, before anyone approves

Adds the requested hours to the hours already on the schedule for that workweek. The approver sees the new weekly total and exactly how many of those hours fall past 40.
fields.feature_2:
Cost at time and a half on every request

Prices each request from the employee's hourly rate, multiplied by 1.5 for overtime, and puts the dollar figure beside the hours. Managers approve a cost, not only a count.
fields.feature_3:
Overtime budgets by cost center

Charges each approved request to a cost center and tracks what is left of its monthly overtime budget. A request that would overspend goes to a second approver in finance.
fields.feature_4:
A weekly cap you set

Holds any request that would push someone past the weekly limit you choose, such as 50 hours. The supervisor sees why it was held and can offer the shift to someone else.
fields.feature_5:
Call-in hours filed after the fact

Lets employees file hours they already worked, like a call-in at night, with the reason attached. Those entries are marked apart from approved requests, and payroll gets them.
fields.feature_6:
Your code, your request history

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub on paid plans along with the table of every request and decision. Your engineers can extend it or connect it to a scheduling tool later on.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Ways Teams Approve Extra Hours
fields.tab_content_1:
All three pickers checked against 50 hours

Harlow Distribution caps pickers at 50 hours a week, overtime included. A shift lead asks for three pickers on a 10-hour Saturday, and the form adds it to each scheduled week. Two come out at 50 and go to the operations manager. Tom Becker is already at 44. Saturday would take him to 54, and the form holds him.
fields.tab_content_2:
Boiler repair priced at time and a half

Boilers do not wait for Monday. At Pinecrest Apartments, tech Marcus Hill asks for 6 hours on Saturday to replace a pump. At his overtime rate of $42.00, that comes to $252.00. Cost center 610 has spent $1,640 of its $2,000 overtime budget this month, and Elena Park, the property manager, approves it alone.
fields.tab_content_3:
When nobody could approve it in advance

The conveyor at Ridgefield Bakery stopped at 11 p.m. Ray Dunn, the mechanic on call, came in and fixed it with no one around to approve the hours. Next morning he files 3 hours from his phone with the work order. His supervisor, Joy Adams, confirms them, and payroll pays them as call-in overtime.
fields.tab_content_4:
The Saturday shift, offered by overtime count

Bayside Health offers each extra Saturday shift in its call center to the agent with the fewest overtime hours this quarter. A supervisor posts an 8-hour shift. Priya Nair has 2 overtime hours, the fewest on the team, and the offer reaches her in Slack first. If she passes, it goes to Luis Ortega, who has 6.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Overtime Request Form
fields.howto_description: Most overtime gets decided in a hallway. Before you write the prompt, settle who approves extra hours and where the limits sit.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Fix the workweek and the cap
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the reasons overtime comes up on your team: a late truck, a sick call, a month-end close, a machine down. Turn them into a short dropdown. Six months later, the counts show which causes cost the most hours.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Note when your workweek starts, for example Sunday at midnight. Overtime is counted one workweek at a time, with no averaging. Federal law puts no weekly limit on hours for workers 16 and older. Any cap, such as 50 hours, is your company's own.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Most requests come from supervisors, and the direct manager usually approves them. Name the point where a second approver joins, such as a request that would overspend the monthly budget, and say whether that person sits in finance or operations.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Point the form at wherever each person's hourly rate and scheduled hours live. Emergent can connect to your scheduling or payroll tool through its API, or keep both tables in the app's own database if you track them by hand today.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the form in a prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Tell Emergent which fields the form needs, what the cap and the budgets are, and who approves each case. Emergent builds the form and its approval steps, and you can change any of it later by asking in plain English.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Federal law says overtime that was worked must be paid, even when nobody approved it in advance. Give employees a way to file those hours afterward with a reason, and let the form record them instead of rejecting them.
fields.howto_step_7_des: File one request that breaks the weekly cap and one call-in from the night before. Check that the first is held with a reason and the second reaches a supervisor. Then look for both rows in the request table.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is blank paper: a Delta College PDF, a 1984 USDA form, the Kansas Adjutant General's sheet, SHRM's sample, a Scribd upload, a Pinterest board and a $0.99 digital form. Each asks for the date, hours and reason and ends at a supervisor's signature. None of them knows how many hours the person is already scheduled for, what the extra hours cost or whether the department has budget left. This page answers the searcher's questions (how to ask, how to justify it, what the 2026 rule is) with federal sources and no legal advice, then builds the form that does the checking before anyone signs: hours added to the scheduled week, a weekly cap, cost at time and a half against a cost center budget, call-ins filed after the fact, and a fair rotation for who gets offered the shift.
tab_stories: A warehouse shift lead asks for three pickers to work a 10-hour Saturday; the form adds the shift to each picker's scheduled week and holds the one who would reach 54 hours against the company's 50-hour cap.

An apartment maintenance tech asks for 6 hours to replace a boiler pump; the form prices the hours at time and a half on his $28.00 rate, finds room in the cost center's $2,000 monthly overtime budget and sends it to the property manager alone.

A bakery mechanic is called in at 11 p.m. when the oven conveyor stops, fixes it with no one around to approve the hours, and files 3 hours from his phone the next morning; his supervisor confirms them and payroll pays them as call-in overtime.
A patient call center fills an 8-hour Saturday shift by offering it first to the agent with the fewest overtime hours this quarter, and the offer goes to her in Slack.

claims_to_source: Under the FLSA, covered nonexempt employees must receive overtime pay of at least one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek
An employer announcement that overtime will not be paid unless authorized in advance does not remove the employee's right to be paid for overtime hours actually worked
A workweek is a fixed, regularly recurring period of 168 hours, and each workweek stands alone; hours cannot be averaged across two or more workweeks
The FLSA does not limit the number of hours per day or days per week an employer may require of an employee aged 16 or older, or the number of overtime hours that may be scheduled

In May 2026 the Department of Labor removed the vacated 2024 overtime rule from the regulations and republished the earlier text, so the standard salary level for the white-collar exemptions is $684 per week
To be exempt from overtime as an executive, administrative or professional employee, a worker must be paid a salary of at least $684 per week and meet a duties test
Colleges and state agencies post overtime request forms as PDFs for their own staff (for example Delta College and the Kansas Adjutant General's Department)
